topics.title: PIREPs (pilot weather reports)
lesson: A pilot weather report (PIREP) is an observation made by a pilot in flight. Transport Canada calls PIREPs the only direct source of information on cloud heights, turbulence, visibility, winds and icing between weather stations. They matter most on flights below 10,000 ft. Reports of conditions worse than forecast are the most valuable.

list: Location and altitude (heights are normally above sea level), UTC time and aircraft type.
Cloud tops and upper layers, cruising-level winds, and anything that differs significantly from the forecast.
Low cloud, reduced visibility, icing, and convective activity such as wind shear, squall lines, turbulence, thunderstorms and cumulonimbus.

Turbulence: intensity, whether in or near cloud, altitude and duration if it applies. Icing: intensity and type, altitude and indicated airspeed. Wind shear: the loss or gain of airspeed and the altitude where it happened.
Regular PIREPs carry the heading UACN10. Urgent PIREPs (heading UACN01, or UUA) are for atmospheric conditions that are an immediate hazard for all aviation users.
Examples the AIM names as urgent: clear air turbulence encountered, and volcanic ash detected.
A hazardous PIREP under one hour old is broadcast at once to aircraft in the affected area and repeated in later scheduled broadcasts. It may also lead to a SIGMET.

lesson: Pilots file with a flight information centre (FIC) on an en route frequency, or by toll-free call after landing. Flight service passes the report at once on meteorological circuits to air traffic services units and the Canadian Meteorological Aviation Centres (CMAC). ECCC meteorologists use PIREPs to confirm or amend forecasts.

list: Turbulence. Light: momentary, slight, erratic changes in altitude or attitude. Moderate: like light but more intense. Severe: large, abrupt changes in altitude or attitude.

Icing. Light: the accumulation rate could become a problem over a long flight. Moderate: even a short exposure could be a hazard, so de-icing equipment or a diversion is needed. Severe: de-icing or anti-icing equipment fails to reduce or control the hazard.

lesson: The element order in the US FAA format is: message type (UA or UUA), /OV location, /TM time (UTC), /FL altitude or flight level, /TP aircraft type, /SK sky condition, /WX flight visibility and weather, /TA temperature, /WV wind, /TB turbulence, /IC icing, /RM remarks. The Canadian example in the AIM shows the same fields. Altitude may be given as DURD, DURC or UNKN.

lesson.note: Study the Canadian outline on the back cover of the Canada Flight Supplement for the exact layout. This lesson takes the full element order from the FAA, so confirm it against the Canadian source.

terms: PIREP
Pilot weather report: an in-flight observation of weather by a pilot.
UUA / UACN01
Urgent PIREP heading, for conditions that are an immediate hazard to all aviation users.
UACN10
Heading of a regular PIREP in the AIM example.
FIC
Flight information centre. Takes PIREPs by radio or phone and passes them on.
CMAC
Canadian Meteorological Aviation Centres. Receive PIREPs from flight service.
/TB, /IC
Turbulence and icing elements of the PIREP.

questions.q: According to Transport Canada, why are PIREPs important?
c: They are the only direct source of cloud height, turbulence, visibility, wind and icing data between weather stations
They replace the hourly METAR at any aerodrome that has no observer, so no other report is needed there
They are the main source of surface pressure for the numerical models that ECCC runs every day, which makes them vital
They are filed by every aircraft on every flight, whatever the weather, so every flight has a complete record
questions.e: Transport Canada PIREP page and TP 2228E-9.

questions.q: Which PIREPs does Transport Canada call the most valuable?
c: Reports of conditions worse than forecast
Reports that match the forecast exactly
Reports of smooth air and clear sky only, from any level
Reports filed only by airline crews above FL250, since they fly the highest and see the most weather
questions.e: Transport Canada: clear reports on worse-than-forecast conditions are vital.

questions.q: PIREPs are particularly important on flights below:
c: FL250, because heavy jet traffic rarely stops to report anything above that level

questions.q: Which headings mark a regular and an urgent PIREP in the AIM?
c: UACN10 regular; UACN01 or UUA urgent
UACN01 regular; UACN10 urgent
UACN10 for both, with the urgency shown only in the remarks section
SACN10 regular and SACN01 urgent, using the same headings as the surface observation bulletins

questions.q: An urgent PIREP is issued for conditions that are:
c: An immediate hazard for all aviation users
Merely different from the forecast
Reported by a pilot with more than 5,000 hours
Expected to occur within the next 24 hours, whether or not any aircraft has met them yet

questions.q: What happens to a hazardous PIREP less than one hour old?
c: It is broadcast at once to aircraft in the affected area and repeated in later broadcasts
It is held until the next scheduled METAR, then sent with it
It is stored for the monthly climate summary and not broadcast
It is passed on only to the pilot who filed it, who must relay it to any other aircraft by radio

questions.q: How does a pilot file a PIREP?
c: With a FIC on an en route frequency, or by toll-free call after landing
Only by mailing the report to the nearest MWO after the flight
Only through the aircraft's flight data recorder after landing, at the home base of the operator
By sending a TAF amendment request to the aerodrome

questions.q: Where do PIREPs received by flight service go next?
c: Straight onto meteorological circuits, and to ATS units and the CMAC
Into a paper file that is reviewed at the end of each month by the regional office
Only to the aerodrome that the pilot departed from
To the airline dispatcher, and to no one else

questions.q: PIREP heights in the AIM are normally stated as:
c: Height above sea level
Height above the ground at the aerodrome of departure
Pressure altitude in millibars
Flight levels only, even when the aircraft is below the transition altitude near the ground

questions.q: In the FAA PIREP format, which element comes directly after /TM?
c: /FL, altitude or flight level
/OV, location
/TP, aircraft type
/WX, because flight visibility must be known before the aircraft altitude is stated
questions.e: FAA JO 7110.10X, Ch. 9 Sec. 2 (2014): order is UA/UUA, /OV, /TM, /FL, /TP, /SK, /WX, /TA, /WV, /TB, /IC, /RM. US source.

questions.q: Transport Canada defines light turbulence as:
c: Momentary, slight, erratic changes in altitude or attitude
Large, abrupt changes in altitude or attitude
Turbulence like moderate but weaker, felt only in cloud
Steady, smooth bumps that last for several minutes and never change the attitude of the aircraft

questions.q: Transport Canada defines moderate icing as:
c: Even a short exposure could be a hazard, so de-icing equipment or a diversion is needed
The accumulation rate may become a problem over a long flight
De-icing or anti-icing equipment fails to control the hazard
Ice that forms only on the propeller or the windshield and never builds up on the wings or tail

questions.q: Transport Canada defines severe icing as:
c: De-icing or anti-icing equipment fails to reduce or control the hazard
The rate of accumulation may become a problem on a long flight
Even a short exposure could be a hazard
Any ice accumulation above 5 mm on the wings, whether or not the aircraft can still be controlled

questions.q: What can a hazardous PIREP lead to?
c: A SIGMET issued by an MWO
A change to the climate normals
A new METAR code table
An automatic amendment of every TAF in the same FIR, since forecasters must copy any report they receive

questions.q: A pilot detects volcanic ash. What should the pilot do?
c: File an urgent PIREP with the nearest ATS unit
Wait and report it with the post-flight paperwork
Report it only if the ash reaches the cabin
Climb above the layer and report it after landing, to avoid delaying the flight with radio calls

sources: Transport Canada, Pilot reports (PIREPs) page (2026-11-02 fetch): purpose, below 10,000 ft, worse-than-forecast, content list
Transport Canada TP 2228E-9, PIREPs (2026-11-02 fetch): turbulence and icing intensity wording; format outline is on the Canada Flight Supplement back cover and was not read
Transport Canada AIM 2023-1 MET (2026-11-02 fetch, first 100,000 characters): MET 1.1.6.1, 1.2.2, 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4, 2.5, Table 2.1
FAA Order JO 7110.10X Ch. 9 Sec. 2 (2014, US): PIREP element order and urgent criteria (TC wording confirms the same field set)
unverified: The AIM edition read is 2023-1; later editions were not checked, and the last 6,800 characters of the document were not read.
The /WX element and the full element order are confirmed from the FAA source only. The Canadian table was seen in summary and lists /TM, /FL, /TP, /SK, /TA, /WV, /TB, /IC, /RM.

The US list of urgent criteria (tornado, severe turbulence or icing, hail, low-level wind shear, volcanic activity) is not taught as Canadian practice; the AIM names only clear air turbulence and volcanic ash in the part read.
Wording of the intensity definitions is paraphrased from TP 2228E-9; the AIM's own turbulence and icing tables were not compared.

topics.title: Obstructions to vision
lesson: An obstruction to vision is a phenomenon other than precipitation (the weather class) that can reduce horizontal visibility near the ground. The US observing manual lists fog, ground fog, ice fog, haze, smoke, dust, blowing snow, blowing sand, blowing dust and blowing spray. Canadian observers report them with the rules below.

list: General (6.7.1): an obstruction is recorded only when the prevailing visibility is 6 SM or less.
Fog (6.7.1.1): reported when visibility at the earth's surface is reduced to 1/2 SM or less.
Mist (6.7.1.3): reported when visibility is reduced to between 5/8 and 6 SM inclusive.
Haze, dust haze and smoke (6.7.1.6): reported when prevailing visibility is 6 SM or less.
Blowing snow, blowing dust and blowing sand (6.7.1.4): reported when visibility is 6 SM or less and the phenomenon is the only factor reducing it.
Dust storm and sandstorm (6.7.1.5): reported when visibility is 6 SM or less and the phenomenon is the only factor reducing it. They are heavy at 1/4 SM or less.
Freezing fog (6.7.1.2): fog with temperature from -0.1 to -30.0 C and visibility 1/2 SM or less.
Shallow fog (MIFG), fog patches (BCFG) and fog covering part of the aerodrome (PRFG) are reported when visibility is greater than 6 SM (6.8.1).

lesson: The visibility value separates them. At 1/2 SM or less the report is fog. From 5/8 to 6 SM it is mist. Both are produced by water droplets or ice crystals suspended in the air at the surface; haze, smoke and dust are solid particles. See the Fog types topic for formation.

Smoke can also be reported as an obscuring layer: surface-based, aloft, or both (MANOBS 7.2.3.1). A sky that is completely obscured is reported with vertical visibility instead of cloud amount, type and height.

lesson.note: Check the current MANOBS chapter 6 for the full list, intensity rules and METAR codes. This lesson covers the criteria read on 2026-11-02.

terms: Obstruction to vision
Non-precipitation phenomenon that reduces horizontal visibility near the ground, such as fog, haze, smoke, dust or blowing snow.
Mist
Obstruction reported when visibility is 5/8 to 6 SM inclusive (MANOBS).
Fog
Obstruction reported when visibility is 1/2 SM or less at the surface (MANOBS).
MIFG, BCFG, PRFG
Shallow fog, fog patches, and fog covering part of the aerodrome; used when visibility is above 6 SM.
Obscuring layer
Non-cloud layer that wholly or partly blocks the view of the sky or higher clouds.

questions.q: What is an obstruction to vision?
c: A non-precipitation phenomenon that may reduce horizontal visibility near the ground
Any precipitation that falls to the ground and reduces visibility
A cloud layer that has a base below 1,000 ft above the aerodrome level
A measurement error that arises when the visibility sensor is dirty or its lens is covered in frost
questions.e: US observing practice (Federal Meteorological Handbook / Circular N definition, via the AMS glossary page).

questions.q: Which of these is an obstruction to vision?
c: Haze
Rain
Snow
Thunderstorm
questions.e: US list: fog, ground fog, ice fog, blowing snow, sand, dust and spray, haze, smoke, dust. Precipitation is weather-class.

questions.q: MANOBS records an obstruction to vision only when prevailing visibility is:
c: 6 SM or less
3 SM or less
1 SM or less
15 SM or less, which is the maximum value that a Canadian station can report

questions.q: Fog is reported when the visibility at the surface is reduced to:
c: 1/2 SM or less
3/4 SM or less
1 SM or less
6 SM or less, provided that the sky overhead is completely obscured at the same time

questions.q: Mist is reported when visibility is reduced to:
c: 5/8 to 6 SM inclusive
1/2 SM or less
Below 1/4 SM only
Between 7 and 15 SM, so long as the humidity is above 90 percent

questions.q: Suspended water droplets cut the prevailing visibility to 3/8 SM. What is reported?
c: Fog
Mist
Haze
Blowing spray, because water is the only cause of the reduction in visibility
questions.e: MANOBS 6.7.1.1: fog at 1/2 SM or less.

questions.q: Suspended water droplets cut the prevailing visibility to 3 SM. What is reported?
c: Mist
Fog
Freezing fog
Fog patches, because the visibility is more than 1/2 SM and the cause is the same

questions.q: When is blowing snow reported?
c: Visibility 6 SM or less, and blowing snow is the only factor reducing it
Any time snow is on the ground and the wind is above 10 kt
Only when visibility is below 1/4 SM
Whenever snow is falling and the wind speed is more than 15 kt, no matter what the visibility is

questions.q: A dust storm or sandstorm is heavy when visibility is:
c: 1/4 SM or less
1/2 SM or less
3/4 SM or less
6 SM or less, which is the limit for reporting any dust phenomenon at all

questions.q: When is haze or smoke reported?
c: When prevailing visibility is 6 SM or less
Only when visibility is below 1/2 SM
Only when visibility is below 3 SM
Only when smoke is seen overhead at the station, whatever the prevailing visibility is

questions.q: Freezing fog is reported at temperatures of:
c: -0.1 to -30.0 C, with visibility 1/2 SM or less
Any temperature below 5 C, with visibility 1 SM or less
0 to 5 C, with visibility 1/2 SM or less
Below -30 C only, because ice fog forms at a lower temperature and replaces it

questions.q: MIFG, BCFG and PRFG are used when visibility is:
c: Greater than 6 SM
1/2 SM or less
Exactly 1/4 SM
Between 5/8 and 6 SM, in the same range as mist

questions.q: Is rain an obstruction to vision?
c: No. It is precipitation, which belongs to the weather class
Yes, whenever it reduces visibility below 6 SM
Yes, but only when it is heavy
Yes, but only when it freezes on contact, at which point it is reclassified as an obstruction
questions.e: US definition: obstructions are phenomena other than the weather class.

questions.q: How can smoke be reported in the sky condition?
c: As a surface-based obscuring layer, a layer aloft, or both
Only as a layer aloft
Never. It belongs only in present weather
Only as low cloud, using the cloud type that has the nearest base height

sources: MANOBS 8th ed. Am. 3, Chapter 6 sections 6.7.1 to 6.7.1.6 and 6.8.1 (2026-11-02 fetch of the canada.ca HTML edition, summarized by the fetch tool): thresholds
MANOBS 7.2.3, 7.2.3.1 (obscuring layer, smoke) from the same fetch
US definition and list of obstructions to vision: glossary page that cites the US Manual of Surface Observations (WBAN), Circular N (2026-11-02 fetch); the page does not attribute it to the AMS
unverified: The threshold values were read through the fetch tool's summary of the MANOBS web page, not from a direct page image. Confirm the section numbers and values against the PDF.
Intensity rules for each obstruction, METAR/SPECI codes (BR, FG, HZ, FU, DU, BLSN and so on) and sub-types were not read in this pass.
Fog versus haze cause (droplets versus solid particles) is general knowledge, not a fetched statement.
The obstruction list is the US list; MANOBS's own list in Chapter 6 was not read in full.

topics.title: Sky condition and cloud height reporting
lesson: Sky condition is the observer's description of cloud layers and obscuring phenomena above the station. Each layer is reported with its amount and the height of its base. All heights are in feet (1 ft is exactly 0.3048 m).

list: Reference level (7.3.1): at airports, heights are measured from the official aerodrome level. Elsewhere they are measured from ground level at the observing station.
Increments (7.3): heights of layers and vertical visibility are reported in 100 ft steps up to and including 10,000 ft, and in 1,000 ft steps above that.
If a layer height falls between two reportable values, report the lower one. If a cloud amount falls between two reportable values, report the greater one.
If the sky is completely obscured, report vertical visibility instead of cloud amount, type and height.
Ceiling (7.2.7): the lowest layer aloft reported as broken or overcast, or the vertical visibility.
Obscuring layer (7.2.3): a non-cloud layer, such as smoke, that wholly or partly blocks the view of the sky or higher clouds.

lesson: MANOBS Table 7-1 is the guide to the approximate base height of each cloud type. It is in the Cloud classification topic. Use it as a guide, not as a measurement.

list: A laser ceilometer points a pulse straight up and times the light scattered back from the cloud base. It sees only what is overhead.

US ASOS example (NWS page, archived, about 1990s figures): the sensor reports layers up to 12,000 ft, uses 30-second samples, and every minute processes the last 30 minutes of data with the latest 10 minutes counted twice, so it follows current changes. It can report up to three layers.
Canadian AWOS ceilometers report cloud bases up to 25,000 ft (Surface observing topic).

Limits: it does not see cap clouds over distant mountains or low cloud over nearby water. Fog or precipitation can mask the signal and give a false layer. Thin layers such as virga or scud may be reported when a human would ignore them. It lags in rapid change, so check later reports.

lesson.note: Heights above the reference level, in feet, rounded down. Amounts rounded up. Keep those two rules apart.

terms: Ceiling
Lowest layer aloft reported as broken or overcast, or the vertical visibility (MANOBS 7.2.7).
Vertical visibility
Reported instead of cloud when the sky is completely obscured.
Reference level
Official aerodrome level at airports; ground level at the station elsewhere.
Ceilometer
Instrument that measures cloud base height, usually with a laser pointed up.
Obscuring layer
Non-cloud layer that blocks the view of the sky or of higher clouds.

questions.q: At an airport, cloud heights are measured from:
c: The official aerodrome level
Mean sea level
The level of the observer's eyes
The highest terrain within 5 SM, whichever is the greatest

questions.q: At a non-airport station, cloud heights are measured from:
c: Ground level at the observing station
The official aerodrome level of the nearest airport
Mean sea level
The roof of the station building, since that is where the observer's instruments are mounted

questions.q: Cloud heights up to and including 10,000 ft are reported in steps of:
c: 100 ft
500 ft
50 ft, the finest step that the aviation observing standard allows for any height

questions.q: Cloud heights above 10,000 ft are reported in steps of:
c: 100 ft
500 ft
5,000 ft, which is the step used for high cloud at every observing station in Canada

questions.q: A layer base is between two reportable heights. Which value is reported?
c: The lower one
The higher one
The average of the two
Whichever is nearer to the next flight level that the pilot has filed for the route

questions.q: A cloud amount falls between two reportable values. Which is reported?
c: The greater one
The smaller one
The average, rounded to the nearest eighth
Whichever is closer to the amount seen at the previous observation on the hour

questions.q: What is reported when the sky is completely obscured?
c: Vertical visibility, in place of cloud amount, type and height
Overcast at 0 ft
The height of the highest cloud seen on the last report
Clear sky, because no cloud can be identified, together with the visibility

questions.q: How does MANOBS define the ceiling?
c: The lowest layer aloft reported as broken or overcast, or the vertical visibility
The lowest cloud of any amount
The highest overcast layer in the sky
The height of the lowest scattered layer or the vertical visibility, whichever is the greater of the two

questions.q: What is an obscuring layer?
c: A non-cloud layer that wholly or partly blocks the view of the sky or higher clouds
A cloud layer with a base below 500 ft that is reported as the ceiling at the aerodrome
A cloud layer seen only on satellite images
Any cloud layer that covers more than 4/8 of the sky, whatever its height or type

questions.q: How does a laser ceilometer find a cloud base?
c: It sends pulses straight up and times the light scattered back
It measures the temperature at which the cloud forms, then calculates the height
It uses the dew point depression at the surface to estimate the height
It scans the horizon with a rotating beam and measures the angle to the base of the cloud
questions.e: NWS ASOS sky page (archived): laser pulses, backscatter sorted into height bins.

questions.q: In the ASOS example, why are the last 10 minutes of data counted twice?
c: So the report follows current changes in the sky
So the sensor can see layers above 12,000 ft
To remove the effect of precipitation on the signal
To make up for the sensor's inability to see layers more than 3 SM away from the station
questions.e: NWS ASOS sky page (archived, US, undated, 1990s figures).

questions.q: A ceilometer is a poor sensor for which situation?
c: Cap cloud over distant mountains
Overcast cloud directly over the sensor
A solid overcast with a base at 800 ft
A broken layer at 3,000 ft passing overhead, because the sensor loses the signal beyond 2,000 ft
questions.e: NWS ASOS sky page: it reports only weather that passes over the sensor.

questions.q: Where do you find the approximate base heights by cloud type?
c: MANOBS Table 7-1
The standard atmosphere table
The station plot
The TAF validity period, since forecasters list base heights there for each cloud type
questions.e: MANOBS 7.3.1; see the Cloud classification topic.

questions.q: Cloud base heights in MANOBS are given in:
c: Feet
Metres
Hectopascals
Flight levels, from the surface up to the top of the highest layer reported
questions.e: MANOBS conventions: references for cloud base height are in feet (0.3048 m).

NWS ASOS Sky Condition page (US, archived 2008, figures from the 1990s) for the ceilometer principle, sampling and limits
Cloud classification topic (Moisture 2) for MANOBS Table 7-1 heights, verified earlier
